what_it_does: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is an AI architecture that scales models to trillions of parameters by routing each input token to only a small 'specialist' sub-network rather than running the full model — so compute stays fixed even as the model grows enormous. The catch is that these specialists live on different GPUs, so every forward pass requires sending tokens across the network to reach the right specialist, then sending results back. That inter-GPU communication currently eats up 47% of total runtime. This paper presents COMET, a system that hides communication latency behind computation by overlapping the two at a much finer granularity than previous approaches, achieving a 1.96x speedup on a single MoE layer and 1.71x end-to-end.
method_in_detail:
The idea. When GPU A is sending tokens to GPU B's specialist, GPU A's specialist should simultaneously be doing math on the tokens it already received. Existing systems do this at a coarse level — split work into two big chunks and pipeline them — but the two halves don't fit together neatly in time, leaving the GPU idle at the start and end of each chunk.

How it works — shared tensor dependency resolving. Each MoE layer has a shared buffer (called a shared tensor) that one operation writes into and the next reads from. COMET analyzes exactly which rows or columns of that buffer are independent of each other: in the first half of the MoE layer (dispatching tokens to specialists), different tokens don't depend on each other, so the buffer can be split row-by-row and specialists can begin their large matrix multiply (the core math: multiplying weight matrices by token vectors, which the paper calls GEMM for 'general matrix multiply') as each token arrives rather than waiting for all of them. In the second half (collecting results back), the top-K reduction (picking the best results from the experts each token visited) requires all columns of the output to be complete before reducing, so the buffer is split column-by-column instead, and the send-back operation starts as soon as the first batch of columns is ready. Within each split, computation tiles are reordered to always process locally available data first, hiding remote data transfers behind local math.

How it works — adaptive workload assignment. Communication and computation are bundled into a single fused GPU program (a 'kernel') rather than two separate programs on two separate scheduling queues. Inside this kernel, thread blocks (groups of GPU cores that execute together) are partitioned into dedicated compute groups and dedicated communication groups. The ratio of compute to communication thread blocks is profiled offline for each model configuration and sequence length, then selected at runtime from a pre-built table. This prevents the two from interfering with each other's hardware resources and avoids the scheduling jitter that plagued prior kernel-level approaches.

The key design choice. Fusing everything into one kernel with thread-block specialization is what enables the fine-grained overlap: the communication groups can start moving the next batch of tokens the instant the computation groups free those rows in the shared buffer, rather than waiting for an OS-level kernel launch.

The result. On 8 NVIDIA H800 GPUs running Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen2-MoE, and Phi3.5-MoE models, COMET hides 86.5% of communication latency on average (versus 29% and 69% for the two best prior systems) while fully preserving the math unit efficiency of the expert computations. It has been deployed in a production cluster of over ten thousand GPUs, saving millions of GPU-hours.
